newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wheat exports back in spotlight after EU move.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wheat exports back in spotlight after EU move.

text.p: U.S. wheat will be back at the center of world wheat export trade this summer after the end of European Union weekly wheat tenders for the current season to July, industry analysts and exporters said.

"If exports out of Europe are suspended, it would most definitely affect our U.S. wheat exports," a senior U.S. wheat export trader said. "There is no alternative but the U.S. when you are talking July, August and September (positions)."
"Australia was supposedly almost all sold out. Argentina is sold out and now Europe is saying they are suspending," the trader said.

"Personally, I am happy about this but people who are short the board aren't. This is creating exports for new-crop time which is exactly what we need. We were in the doldrums," the export trader said.
The EU ended the bulk of its July/June wheat export sales on Thursday by closing its weekly tender system. But it left the door ajar to exporters seeking last-minute supplies.

Thursday's decision coincided with fresh awards that added at least 400,000 tonnes to the volume released for export and pushed this season's sales above 9.6 million tonnes. An EU official said it may allow another 70,000 tonnes on Friday.

But even if a limited amount of additional sales appear from the EU before the start of the new season in July, the halt to weekly tenders cemented ideas that European officials are worried about potential damage from dry weather on the next French crop and this week's winterkill in U.S. wheat.
Chicago Board of Trade May wheat futures shot up the 20-cent per bushel daily limit on the news.
"The EU action is really the catalyst for this," said analyst Charlie Sernatinger at Man International.
"It exacerbates an already tight supply situation worldwide. Basically, it is just us and Canada as the sole remaining sellers in the world until October," he said.

Joe Victor, vice president of marketing for Allendale Inc, said the EU action intensifies the concerns about supplies, particularly after agronomists said two days of freezing temperatures last weekend severely damaged U.S. winter wheat.
"As long as we have uncertainty in that wheat (damage) estimate, the only thing we can do is grind it higher," Victor said, referring to higher prices.
Victor said the EU's action was preceded on Monday by a reduction in its duties on distant wheat imports, a clear sign it was concerned about dry weather cutting the current crop.
"They have to make sure they have enough domestic supplies to feed their own countries," Victor said.
The EU move also means the world market is probably headed back up toward the high level of U.S. prices, tarders said.
"It improves our prospects to pick up export business," a second U.S. exporter said. "We are depending on our new crop.

"Our stocks are tight in the old crop but there is still wheat around here and there and the new crop is not all that far off," he said, referring to U.S. winter wheat harvest supplies that will start appearing in June.
"Whether we reap the benefits or not it still remains to be seen. It comes down if the buyers want to chase this market or not," the exporter said.
